## Nagel: consciousness as subjective point of view

Thomas Nagel argues that consciousness includes an essentially first-person character that cannot be captured by purely objective description. His famous formulation is that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something that it is like to be that organism.” For Nagel, even a complete physical account of a bat’s nervous system would omit the bat’s lived perspective. The hard problem, in this view, is not merely explaining functions such as discrimination or report; it is explaining subjective experience itself.

## Dennett: dissolving the “hard” problem

Daniel Dennett is skeptical that there is a further mysterious property left over after we explain cognition, behavior, access, memory, and report. He warns against treating inner experience as a private object beyond scientific analysis, writing, “There is no such thing as philosophy-free science; there is only science whose philosophical baggage is taken on board without examination.” Dennett’s project examines the assumptions that make qualia seem ineffable and argues that careful functional explanation can dissolve the apparent gap.

## Comparison

Nagel thinks objective methods leave out subjectivity; Dennett thinks the supposed leftover is partly produced by misleading intuitions about introspection. Nagel emphasizes epistemic limits: third-person science cannot fully tell us what experience is like from the inside. Dennett emphasizes methodological discipline: if a feature makes no difference to capacities, reports, or dispositions, we should question whether it has been coherently identified.

## Synthesis

Their primary divergence is whether subjective “what-it-is-like” character is an irreducible datum demanding explanation, or a confused target that becomes tractable once consciousness is analyzed through public, functional, and interpretive methods.
